summary: What audit redaction keeps of a value: the credential-key rules, the identifier exemption, every value pattern in order, and hash_only. Checked through each engine's redaction function; no engine instance is started. Provider-shaped samples break their prefix with one \u escape so that repository secret scanners skip them; the parsed strings are unchanged.

cases.summary: A key containing pass, secret, token, authorization or authorisation, cookie, api key, credential or private key (with _, - or nothing between two words) anywhere, in any case, has its value replaced by [redacted], whatever the value's type.
Credential words match inside longer keys, so these ordinary names are redacted too; keyword is kept because key alone is not a credential word.

Short names (otp, totp, hotp, mfa, 2fa, pin, session, private, auth, cvv, cvc) redact as whole key segments: keys split at separators, at camelCase humps and after acronyms, and compare in lower case.
Keys that only contain or extend a short name are kept.
Segments follow [A-Z]+[0-9]*(?![a-z])|[A-Z]?[a-z0-9]+ with its backtracking: PINs is PI and Ns, 2FA is 2 and FA, digits join the letters before them (MFA2, Pin2), and PIN12def is PIN1 and 2def.
When a key's last segment names an identifier or digest, its value keeps long hexadecimal and base64url runs; other keys lose them.
Only a whole last segment counts: ETag splits into E and Tag, userid is one word, and ids_count and hash_value end in other words. Ids, Id and messageID end in identifier segments.
Arrays inherit the identifier exemption from their key; every key of a nested object decides it afresh.
The identifier exemption covers only the two random-run rules; every other value pattern still applies.
A private key block is replaced from its BEGIN line through the first END line naming any private key type, or to the end of the text when none follows; the markers are case-sensitive.

cases.summary: A JSON web token is a base64url header and payload that both start with eyJ, then a possibly empty signature; it must not follow a base64url character.
A web address keeps its scheme, user and host but loses the password before @; the scheme starts at a word boundary and has at most 31 characters.
A credential-named parameter after ?, & or ; loses its value up to &, #, whitespace, a quote, < or >; names compare without case.

A credential label not preceded by a letter or digit, then an optional quote and : or = with spaces or tabs around it, loses its value: a whole quoted string keeps its quotes; otherwise the value runs to whitespace, a quote, a comma, ;, &, < or >. The value must start on the label's line.

An Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, X-Api-Key or X-Auth-Token header, or a Cookie or Set-Cookie header whose value starts with name=, keeps its name, quoting and scheme and loses its value up to the closing quote or the line end.
Bearer then spaces or tabs, at a word boundary, hides a token of 16 or more characters, with its = padding, when the token has a digit or at least 32 characters.

GitHub tokens (ghp_, gho_, ghu_, ghs_ and ghr_ with 20 or more letters and digits, or github_pat_ with 22 or more letters, digits and underscores) are replaced when no letter, digit or underscore touches either end.
Slack tokens (xoxa-, xoxb-, xoxp-, xoxr- and xoxs- with 10 or more letters, digits and dashes) are replaced unless a letter, digit or dash precedes them; an underscore ends the token.
Amazon Web Services access key identifiers (AKIA or ASIA and 16 capitals or digits) are replaced when no letter or digit touches either end.

sk- keys with 20 or more characters, sk_ and rk_ live or test keys with 16 or more, and AIza keys of exactly 39 characters, with no base64url character touching either end, are replaced only when they contain a digit; a 40-character run can still meet the base64url rule.
A Telegram bot token (optional bot, 6 to 12 digits, a colon, then 30 or more base64url characters) keeps its number and loses the rest.
A run of 32 or more hexadecimal characters with both a digit and a letter, not touching another letter or digit, is replaced.
A run of 40 or more base64url characters that mixes capitals, small letters and digits is replaced when its letter and digit pieces average under three characters.
Patterns apply in order, each to the previous one's output, so a later pattern can widen an earlier replacement, and a match a callback keeps still consumes its text.
Strings at any depth under a key named in hash_only, compared without case, become their length in code points and the first 16 hexadecimal digits of the SHA-256 of their scrubbed UTF-8 text.
Text outside ASCII passes through, and patterns next to it behave the same in both engines when no Unicode space, word character or case fold decides the match.
A top-level string is scrubbed as if under a non-identifier key, numbers, booleans and null are kept, and keys themselves are never scrubbed.
Python's \s, \b and case-insensitive matching are Unicode-aware; the native scanners use ASCII classes.

divergence.reason: Python's \s includes the no-break space, which ends the value; the native scanner continues to the end.
Python's \S refuses the no-break space as the first value character; the native scanner accepts it.
Python's \b sees é as a word character, so bearer is not at a word boundary; the native scanner sees a boundary.
Python's case-insensitive matching folds the long s (U+017F) to s; the native scanner folds only A to Z.
Python's credential-key search folds the long s (U+017F) to s; the native search folds only A to Z.
Python lowers names with str.lower(); the native engine lowers only A to Z, so Ñame does not match ñame.
